v: Now there were some present at the same time who told him about the Galileans, whose blood Pilate had mixed with their sacrifices.
Jesus answered them, “Do you think that these Galileans were worse sinners than all the other Galileans, because they suffered such things?
I tell you, no, but unless you repent, you will all perish in the same way.
Or those eighteen, on whom the tower in Siloam fell and killed them; do you think that they were worse offenders than all the men who dwell in Jerusalem?
I tell you, no, but, unless you repent, you will all perish in the same way.”
b: In this passage Jesus responds to people's questions about two tragedies: Pilate's slaughter of the Galileans, and the collapse of the tower of Siloam that killed eighteen people. The people seem to want to know whether these victims suffered such disasters because they were especially wicked. Jesus' answer is clear: these events do not mean the victims were more guilty than others, and disaster is not a direct punishment for particular sins.

Through this Jesus teaches us that every one of us needs to repent, and that those who do not repent will perish. He does not offer a simple explanation of cause and effect; he stresses instead the universal need for repentance. Disaster and suffering should lead us to examine our own lives, not to rush to judgment about others. Jesus calls each person to recognize the sin in their own heart and to repent in time, so that they may be spared the ruin of the soul.

Through this passage God tells us that whatever disasters happen on the outside, what truly matters is whether our hearts are repentant and cleansed before him. Jesus warns us not to be self-righteous, and not to treat other people's misfortunes as the result of their sins, but to examine ourselves often and seek God's forgiveness and guidance.
q: When you face hardship or disaster in life, are you willing to examine your own life first and repent before God? How can you keep a repentant heart in daily life?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for teaching us to keep a repentant heart at all times. Help us not only to see the faults of others in their suffering, but to examine ourselves, recognize our sin, and seek your forgiveness. May our lives be renewed through repentance and live out your will. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: He spoke this parable. “A certain man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard, and he came seeking fruit on it, and found none.
He said to the vine dresser, ‘Behold, these three years I have come looking for fruit on this fig tree, and found none. Cut it down. Why does it waste the soil?’
He answered, ‘Lord, leave it alone this year also, until I dig around it and fertilize it.
If it bears fruit, fine; but if not, after that, you can cut it down.’ ”
b: In this passage Jesus tells the parable of the fig tree. For three years the tree has produced no fruit, so the owner of the garden decides to cut it down, since it is only wasting the soil. But the gardener pleads with the owner to give the tree one more year, so that he can care for it more attentively, hoping it will bear fruit next year; if not, it can be cut down then.

This parable highlights God's patience and love. The fig tree stands for lives that have borne no spiritual fruit, and God has the right to decide their fate. Yet out of love and mercy he gives us more opportunities to repent and bear fruit. Jesus reminds us that God's patience is sometimes given so that we can bear spiritual fruit under his grace, but that patience is not endless; one day he will judge according to whether our lives have borne fruit.

Through this passage God tells us to treasure the time he gives us and to strive to grow in his grace and bear spiritual fruit. His patience is not permissiveness; it gives us more opportunities to repent and change. We should respond to God's love in time, keep pursuing spiritual growth, and live out his will.
q: Do you see the opportunities for repentance that God has given you? How can you strive to grow and bear spiritual fruit through them?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for giving us the opportunity to repent and grow. Help us to treasure the grace and time you have given and to strive to bear spiritual fruit. May our lives display your glory, and on the day you return may we be called faithful and good servants. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: He was teaching in one of the synagogues on the Sabbath day.
Behold, there was a woman who had a spirit of infirmity eighteen years. She was bent over, and could in no way straighten herself up.
When Jesus saw her, he called her, and said to her, “Woman, you are freed from your infirmity.”
He laid his hands on her, and immediately she stood up straight and glorified God.

The ruler of the synagogue, being indignant because Jesus had healed on the Sabbath, said to the multitude, “There are six days in which men ought to work. Therefore come on those days and be healed, and not on the Sabbath day!”
Therefore the Lord answered him, “You hypocrites! Doesn’t each one of you free his ox or his donkey from the stall on the Sabbath, and lead him away to water?
Ought not this woman, being a daughter of Abraham whom Satan had bound eighteen long years, be freed from this bondage on the Sabbath day?”
As he said these things, all his adversaries were disappointed and all the multitude rejoiced for all the glorious things that were done by him.
b: In this passage we see Jesus healing, on the Sabbath, a woman who had been crippled by a spirit for eighteen years. Her illness bent her over so that she could not stand straight, which pictures how she was bound by suffering and spiritual oppression. Jesus saw her in the synagogue, had compassion on her, and healed her at once, setting her free from her pain. This miracle reveals Jesus' compassion and divine power, and shows that he understood what people truly need on the Sabbath.

However, the synagogue leader was indignant that Jesus healed on the Sabbath, thinking it broke the Sabbath rules. Jesus answered that the true meaning of the Sabbath is people's liberation and freedom, not merely keeping the letter of the rules. He stressed that the Sabbath is not only rest; it is for setting people free from their bondage. Jesus' reply exposed the narrowness of the hypocrites in their religion, and showed that true faith must care about people's needs and deliverance.

Through this passage God tells us that his love and compassion go beyond the limits of the law, and that he cares about the freedom of our souls and lives. Jesus' action shows that God's grace can come to us at any time, not bound by time or regulation. We should follow Jesus' example, placing compassion and love above all rules, and actively doing good in our lives.
q: Have you experienced God's liberation and healing in your life? How can you pass that grace on to others in need?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for the grace of freedom and deliverance. Help us not only to keep the law but to live out our faith in love, and to help those in distress who need your salvation. May we experience your peace and joy every Sabbath. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: He said, “What is God’s Kingdom like? To what shall I compare it?
It is like a grain of mustard seed which a man took and put in his own garden. It grew and became a large tree, and the birds of the sky live in its branches.”
b: In this passage Jesus uses a mustard seed as a picture of the kingdom of God. The mustard seed was one of the smallest seeds people knew at that time, yet when planted in a garden it grows into a large tree, even a place where birds come to nest. Jesus uses this picture to show that although God's kingdom begins small and inconspicuous, when it takes root and grows in the world it shows great influence and power.

This parable highlights the hidden potential and influence of God's kingdom. Its beginning may seem insignificant, but when people plant the seed of faith in their hearts, God's kingdom grows strong in their lives and bears abundant fruit. It also reminds us not to despise small things, because in God's hands even the smallest effort can bear rich fruit.

Through this passage God tells us that although his kingdom begins small in our hearts, as our faith grows it will have great influence in our lives and in the world. We need faith to sow God's word into our lives and to wait patiently for it to grow, until it becomes a source of blessing to others.
q: How do you sow and nurture the kingdom of God in your life? What specific actions could help the seed of your faith grow strong?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for planting your kingdom in our hearts. Help us to nurture this seed of faith patiently so that it grows in our lives and brings a spiritual harvest. May our lives become channels of blessing to others and a witness to your kingdom. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: Again he said, “To what shall I compare God’s Kingdom?
It is like yeast, which a woman took and hid in three measures  of flour, until it was all leavened.”
b: In this passage Jesus again uses a parable to explain the kingdom of God, this time choosing yeast. Yeast is a leavening agent; a small amount works through the whole batch of flour until the entire lump of dough rises. Jesus uses it to describe the character of God's kingdom: it may begin small and unnoticed, but its influence spreads through the whole world.

This parable reminds us that God's kingdom is not merely outward; it is an inward, hidden power. When God's kingdom enters our lives, it changes our whole being and affects every person and thing we touch. This spiritual change is not visible at once, but as time passes its influence appears, and like yeast it finally changes the whole community.

Through this passage God tells us not to despise the small beginning of his kingdom in our hearts, because it has great power to change lives and the world. We should commit ourselves to letting God's kingdom have its influence in our lives; however hidden the process may be, we can trust that God's work will surely bring deep change.
q: Do you see God's kingdom working like yeast in your life? How can you help this process so that God's influence becomes more evident in your life?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for placing the seed of your kingdom in our hearts. Let our lives be filled with your Spirit, and like yeast gradually change us and the people we meet. May our lives bear witness to your power and be part of the spreading of your kingdom. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: He went on his way through cities and villages, teaching, and traveling on to Jerusalem.
One said to him, “Lord, are they few who are saved?” He said to them,
“Strive to enter in by the narrow door, for many, I tell you, will seek to enter in and will not be able.

When once the master of the house has risen up, and has shut the door, and you begin to stand outside and to knock at the door, saying, ‘Lord, Lord, open to us!’ then he will answer and tell you, ‘I don’t know you or where you come from.’
Then you will begin to say, ‘We ate and drank in your presence, and you taught in our streets.’
He will say, ‘I tell you, I don’t know where you come from. Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity.’
There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth when you see Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and all the prophets in God’s Kingdom, and yourselves being thrown outside.
They will come from the east, west, north, and south, and will sit down in God’s Kingdom.
Behold, there are some who are last who will be first, and there are some who are first who will be last.”
b: In this passage someone asks Jesus about being saved, and Jesus' answer stresses that entering the kingdom of God is not easy. He uses the picture of the "narrow door" to describe the way into the kingdom as narrow and hard. Jesus reminds us that entering requires effort; this does not mean relying on our own merit, but following him faithfully and not letting worldly temptations lead us off the right path.

Jesus also warns that many will one day find themselves shut outside because they did not enter the narrow door in time. Those who once assumed they were connected with Jesus, if they have not truly repented and followed the Lord, will face a terrible end. This reminds us that outward religious activity is not enough; true faith requires repentance of heart and lasting obedience.

Through this passage God tells us that entering his kingdom requires sincere faith and tireless effort. We should stay alert and not be complacent over outward religious activity, but keep growing in faith and pursuing a deeper relationship with the Lord, so that we may have a share in his kingdom.
q: Are you striving to enter the narrow door? On your journey of faith, how do you make sure you hold fast to truth and obedience?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for the promise of entering your kingdom. Help us to strive to walk the way of the narrow door and to seek your will every day. May our lives glorify you and finally enjoy eternal life in your kingdom. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: On that same day, some Pharisees came, saying to him, “Get out of here, and go away, for Herod wants to kill you.”
He said to them, “Go and tell that fox, ‘Behold, I cast out demons and perform cures today and tomorrow, and the third day I complete my mission.
Nevertheless I must go on my way today and tomorrow and the next day, for it can’t be that a prophet would perish outside of Jerusalem.’

“Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to her! How often I wanted to gather your children together, like a hen gathers her own brood under her wings, and you refused!
Behold, your house is left to you desolate. I tell you, you will not see me until you say, ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!’ ”
b: In this passage we see some Pharisees trying to warn Jesus of the threat from King Herod, but Jesus is not afraid. He calls Herod a "fox," showing that he sees through Herod's cunning and scheming. Jesus knows his mission and knows clearly that he must carry on his work until it is accomplished in Jerusalem. His response to these warnings shows his firmness and courage; he will not shrink back for anyone or anything.

Jesus then laments over Jerusalem, saying that he often longed to gather the children of that city but they refused. This lament reveals Jesus' deep love and compassion for his people, and also points out that their refusal will bring disastrous consequences. Jesus' words are full of sorrow, because he knows the city's future and the judgment they will face for rejecting him.

Through this passage God tells us that Jesus' love for us is deep and lasting, and even though we often refuse him, he is still willing to receive us back into his arms. This passage also reminds us not to harden our hearts against God's call as Jerusalem did, but to respond sensitively to his love and be willing to find shelter under his wings.
q: When you face challenges in your faith, how do you follow Jesus' courage and firmness? How can you find rest and strength in his love?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for sending Jesus Christ, who showed such courage and firmness in the face of threats and challenges. Help us in difficulty to follow Jesus' example, to walk boldly in your way, and to find shelter in your love. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: When he went into the house of one of the rulers of the Pharisees on a Sabbath to eat bread, they were watching him.
Behold, a certain man who had dropsy was in front of him.
Jesus, answering, spoke to the lawyers and Pharisees, saying, “Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath?”
But they were silent. He took him, and healed him, and let him go.
He answered them, “Which of you, if your son or an ox fell into a well, wouldn’t immediately pull him out on a Sabbath day?”
They couldn’t answer him regarding these things.
b: In this passage Jesus once more challenges the Pharisees' rigid understanding of the law. On the question of whether it is lawful to heal on the Sabbath, Jesus heals a man suffering from dropsy, showing that his interpretation of the law is not mere literal observance but a practice full of love and kindness. His action clearly conveys that God's grace and mercy go far beyond the regulations of the law, and that he cares about people's needs and sufferings.

Jesus' question, "Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath, or not?" left the lawyers and Pharisees speechless, because they understood his point: even on the Sabbath, when someone is in urgent need of help, we should act, and this too is an expression of love. Jesus' words and deeds show us that true faith is not merely keeping the rules but expressing God's love and mercy.

Through this passage God tells us that he wants us to practice love and kindness in life rather than cling to outward form. Jesus' example teaches us to treat others with love always and everywhere, and this is the true way of doing God's will. We should ask ourselves whether we cling too much to form in our lives and neglect to show love and mercy.
q: Are there times in your life when you pay too much attention to form and neglect love and mercy? How can you better practice God's love in daily life?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for sending Jesus Christ, who explained the true meaning of the law through love and mercy. Help us to treat others with the same love and kindness, not merely keeping outward rules but living out the substance of faith. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: He spoke a parable to those who were invited, when he noticed how they chose the best seats, and said to them,
“When you are invited by anyone to a wedding feast, don’t sit in the best seat, since perhaps someone more honorable than you might be invited by him,
and he who invited both of you would come and tell you, ‘Make room for this person.’ Then you would begin, with shame, to take the lowest place.

But when you are invited, go and sit in the lowest place, so that when he who invited you comes, he may tell you, ‘Friend, move up higher.’ Then you will be honored in the presence of all who sit at the table with you.
For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.”
b: In this passage Jesus uses the picture of a wedding feast to teach us the importance of humility. He says that at social occasions we should not scramble for the places of honor, but humbly take the lowest place, so that if the host invites us higher we receive even greater honor. This teaching applies not only to social occasions; it is also a reminder of our attitude before God.

Jesus' parable stresses that the values of God's kingdom differ from those of the world. In the world people often pursue honor and status, but in God's kingdom humility is a vital character quality. Jesus tells us that those who exalt themselves will be humbled, and those who humble themselves will be exalted. So we should learn to remain humble before God, and never exalt ourselves in any situation.

Through this passage God tells us that he values humility of heart, not outward status and honor. When we humble ourselves, God will lift us up in his time. We should always stay humble, not striving for glory for ourselves, but waiting for God's leading and promotion.
q: Are there times in your life when you care too much about worldly honor? How can you stay humble before God and wait for him to lift you up?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for teaching us the importance of humility. Help us to live humbly, not pursuing worldly honor but seeking your pleasure. May we humble ourselves before you and wait for you to lift us up at the right time. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: He also said to the one who had invited him, “When you make a dinner or a supper, don’t call your friends, nor your brothers, nor your kinsmen, nor rich neighbors, or perhaps they might also return the favor, and pay you back.
But when you make a feast, ask the poor, the maimed, the lame, or the blind;
and you will be blessed, because they don’t have the resources to repay you. For you will be repaid in the resurrection of the righteous.”
b: In this passage Jesus teaches us that when we give a feast, we should invite those who cannot repay us, not only those who can. He points out that true blessing comes from selfless giving, especially helping the poor, the disabled, and those in need. This selfless love is one of the core values of God's kingdom.

Jesus' teaching reminds us that often our actions are driven by selfish motives, and we tend to associate with those who can repay us. Yet Jesus tells us that true blessing comes from helping those who cannot repay us, and such actions will be rewarded by God at the resurrection. So we should learn to treat others with selfless love, expecting nothing in return, and then we will truly experience God's grace and blessing.

Through this passage God tells us that selfless love and giving are the essence of God's kingdom. We should treat others with this attitude in our lives, especially those who cannot repay us. When we do, we will receive true blessing in God's kingdom.
q: In your daily life, do you have opportunities to help those who cannot repay you? How can you show God's love in such opportunities?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for teaching us how to treat others with selfless love. Give us a willing heart to give, especially to help those who cannot repay us. May our actions glorify you and receive eternal blessing in your kingdom. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: When one of those who sat at the table with him heard these things, he said to him, “Blessed is he who will feast in God’s Kingdom!”
But he said to him, “A certain man made a great supper, and he invited many people.
He sent out his servant at supper time to tell those who were invited, ‘Come, for everything is ready now.’
They all as one began to make excuses. “The first said to him, ‘I have bought a field, and I must go and see it. Please have me excused.’
“Another said, ‘I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I must go try them out. Please have me excused.’
“Another said, ‘I have married a wife, and therefore I can’t come.’

“That servant came, and told his lord these things. Then the master of the house, being angry, said to his servant, ‘Go out quickly into the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in the poor, maimed, blind, and lame.’
“The servant said, ‘Lord, it is done as you commanded, and there is still room.’
“The lord said to the servant, ‘Go out into the highways and hedges, and compel them to come in, that my house may be filled.
For I tell you that none of those men who were invited will taste of my supper.’ ”
b: In this passage Jesus uses the parable of a great banquet to teach us about the call of God's kingdom. The host prepares a lavish feast, but those invited make all kinds of excuses, and in the end the host gives those places to people overlooked by society. The parable suggests that many people will miss God's grace and call because they are busy with worldly affairs.

Jesus' parable reminds us that the invitation to God's kingdom goes out to everyone, but not everyone will accept it. Those invited refused this precious opportunity because of worldly duties and pleasures, while those willing to respond to God's call, whatever their social standing, will receive a place in his kingdom. This passage urges us not to neglect God's call because of worldly things, for it is an invitation of immeasurable worth.

Through this passage God tells us that his call is for everyone, but only those willing to lay down worldly pursuits can enjoy his grace. We should ask ourselves whether we neglect God's call because of worldly things, and always be ready to answer his invitation and enter his kingdom.
q: Do you sometimes neglect God's call because of worldly affairs? How can you respond better to his invitation and enter his kingdom?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for calling us into your kingdom. Help us not to neglect this precious invitation because of worldly duties and pleasures. May our hearts always be open to you, ready to respond to your call at any time, and may we enjoy the joy of eternal life at the feast of your kingdom. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: Now great multitudes were going with him. He turned and said to them,
“If anyone comes to me, and doesn’t disregard his own father, mother, wife, children, brothers, and sisters, yes, and his own life also, he can’t be my disciple.
Whoever doesn’t bear his own cross, and come after me, can’t be my disciple.
For which of you, desiring to build a tower, doesn’t first sit down and count the cost, to see if he has enough to complete it?
Or perhaps, when he has laid a foundation, and is not able to finish, everyone who sees begins to mock him,
saying, ‘This man began to build, and wasn’t able to finish.’
Or what king, as he goes to encounter another king in war, will not sit down first and consider whether he is able with ten thousand to meet him who comes against him with twenty thousand?
Or else, while the other is yet a great way off, he sends an envoy, and asks for conditions of peace.
So therefore whoever of you who doesn’t renounce all that he has, he can’t be my disciple.
b: In this passage Jesus sets out strict demands for those who follow him. He points out that the cost of following him is very great: disciples must put him first in their lives, above everything, including family and personal interests. Jesus makes clear that being his disciple is not easy; it requires paying a price, carrying the cross, and giving up all worldly possessions.

Jesus' teaching reminds us that following him is not just a decision but a lasting commitment, asking us to give up everything to follow him. He uses the pictures of building a tower and going to war to show that we should seriously count the cost of following him before we decide, because it requires wholehearted devotion. This passage challenges us to consider whether we are truly ready to bear the cost of following Jesus and to put him at the center of our lives.

Through this passage God tells us that a true disciple must put him first in life and be willing to give up everything for him. We should think seriously about our commitment in faith and make sure we are willing to pay the price of following Jesus, so that we can become his true disciples.
q: Are you truly ready to bear the cost of following Jesus? How can you live out this commitment and put Jesus first in your life?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for calling us to be disciples of Jesus Christ. Give us courage and strength to carry the cross and follow him, and to put him first in our lives. May our faith stand the test and glorify your name in every decision. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: Salt is good, but if the salt becomes flat and tasteless, with what do you season it?
It is fit neither for the soil nor for the manure pile. It is thrown out. He who has ears to hear, let him hear.”
b: In this passage Jesus uses the picture of salt to warn us of the danger of faith losing its effect. Salt is an important seasoning, but if it loses its saltiness it is worth nothing and can only be thrown out. Through this Jesus reminds us that as his disciples our lives should be like salt, making an impact in this world so that people experience God's truth and love.

This passage reminds us that faith is not static but needs constant renewal and keeping. We must be on guard against letting the saltiness of our spiritual life fade, which means we need to keep pursuing an intimate relationship with God and put his teachings into practice. If our faith loses its effect, like salt that has lost its saltiness, it will no longer be of any value.

Through this passage God tells us that keeping our spiritual life vital and effective is essential. We should keep examining the state of our faith, making sure we are still exerting a positive influence for God's kingdom. Our lives should be like salt, able to season, preserve, and bless this world.
q: Are you keeping spiritually vital in daily life? How can you make sure your faith has a positive influence in this world?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for reminding us of the importance of faith. Help us to keep our spiritual life vital and to keep influencing this world for your kingdom. May our lives be like salt, letting people experience your love and truth. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: Now all the tax collectors and sinners were coming close to him to hear him.
The Pharisees and the scribes murmured, saying, “This man welcomes sinners, and eats with them.”
He told them this parable.
“Which of you men, if you had one hundred sheep, and lost one of them, wouldn’t leave the ninety-nine in the wilderness, and go after the one that was lost, until he found it?
When he has found it, he carries it on his shoulders, rejoicing.
When he comes home, he calls together his friends and his neighbors, saying to them, ‘Rejoice with me, for I have found my sheep which was lost!’
I tell you that even so there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents, than over ninety-nine righteous people who need no repentance.
b: In this passage Jesus uses the parable of the lost sheep to explain his love for sinners and his eagerness to bring them back. He stresses that God cares not only for those already within his fold, but even more for lost souls. When he finds one lost sinner, heaven is sure to be filled with joy. This passage reflects God's deep love for each of us; however far we have strayed from his way, he never tires of searching for us.

Jesus' parable broke down the self-righteousness of the Pharisees and scribes, emphasizing that God's grace and mercy are boundless, especially toward those lost in sin. He did not come to condemn, but to seek and save the lost. This reminds us that however many mistakes we have made in the past, as long as we repent, God's heart remains open to us.

Through this passage God tells us that he rejoices over every repentant soul. We should ask ourselves whether we have the same care for souls, and live out God's love by actively seeking and helping those who are spiritually lost.
q: Do you see and care for people lost in sin around you? How can you follow Jesus' example in seeking them and helping them find the way back to God?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for your boundless love and mercy; you never give up on a single lost soul. Give us the same love and patience, so that we too may seek and help those who are lost and bring them back into your arms. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: Or what woman, if she had ten drachma coins, if she lost one drachma coin, wouldn’t light a lamp, sweep the house, and seek diligently until she found it?
When she has found it, she calls together her friends and neighbors, saying, ‘Rejoice with me, for I have found the drachma which I had lost.’
Even so, I tell you, there is joy in the presence of the angels of God over one sinner repenting.”
b: In this passage Jesus uses the parable of the lost coin to stress how God treasures every soul. Just as the woman sweeps carefully and searches until she finds her lost coin, God tirelessly searches for every lost soul. When a sinner repents, heaven is filled with joy, showing that in God's eyes each one of us is infinitely precious.

Jesus' parable helps us understand that God has great patience and love for everyone; he will not give up on us even when we make mistakes or stray from his way. This passage reminds us that whatever our past, when we repent God's heart is filled with joy. We too should learn God's love and patience, looking for those around us who need to be found and sharing with them the joy of the gospel.

Through this passage God tells us how precious we are in his eyes. He is willing to spend time and effort searching for us and rejoices over our repentance. We should ask ourselves whether we have this same heart of treasuring and seeking souls, and treat everyone with love and patience.
q: In your life, how do you show that you value and love others? How can you follow God's patience and love in seeking those who need to come back to him?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for treasuring us and being willing to search for us without tiring. Give us the same love, so that in our lives we too may seek and help those who need to return to your arms. May our actions bring joy in heaven. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: He said, “A certain man had two sons.
The younger of them said to his father, ‘Father, give me my share of your property.’ He divided his livelihood between them.
Not many days after, the younger son gathered all of this together and traveled into a far country. There he wasted his property with riotous living.
When he had spent all of it, there arose a severe famine in that country, and he began to be in need.
He went and joined himself to one of the citizens of that country, and he sent him into his fields to feed pigs.
He wanted to fill his belly with the husks that the pigs ate, but no one gave him any.
But when he came to himself he said, ‘How many hired servants of my father’s have bread enough to spare, and I’m dying with hunger!
I will get up and go to my father, and will tell him, “Father, I have sinned against heaven, and in your sight.
I am no more worthy to be called your son. Make me as one of your hired servants.” ’
“He arose, and came to his father. But while he was still far off, his father saw him, and was moved with compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him.
The son said to him, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and in your sight. I am no longer worthy to be called your son.’
“But the father said to his servants, ‘Bring out the best robe, and put it on him. Put a ring on his hand, and sandals on his feet.
Bring the fattened calf, kill it, and let’s eat, and celebrate;
for this, my son, was dead, and is alive again. He was lost, and is found.’ Then they began to celebrate.
b: In this passage Jesus tells the parable of the prodigal son, a powerful portrait of God's boundless grace and love. After leaving his father, the younger son lives recklessly, and in the end has nothing and falls into despair. When he comes to his senses and resolves to go home and confess, his father receives him with unconditional love and forgiveness and celebrates his return with a great feast.

This parable shows deeply that God's love and mercy are unconditional, and his arms are always open waiting for us to return. However great our past mistakes, as long as we repent, God will receive us with boundless love. It shows us that true repentance brings not only personal restoration but touches God's heart, so that heaven too rejoices at our return.

Through this passage God tells us that he is the loving Father who always waits for us to turn back. We should ask ourselves whether we have rebelled and erred like the prodigal, and when needed come before God with a repentant heart. We should believe that God's grace is boundless, and that he is always willing to forgive and give us a new beginning.
q: Is there something in your life that needs repentance? How can you come back into God's arms with the heart of the prodigal and receive his grace and forgiveness?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for your boundless love and grace; however far we have strayed, you are always willing to receive us. Help us to return to you with a repentant heart and to receive your forgiveness and grace. May our lives be renewed by your love and become a witness to your grace. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: “Now his elder son was in the field. As he came near to the house, he heard music and dancing.
He called one of the servants to him, and asked what was going on.
He said to him, ‘Your brother has come, and your father has killed the fattened calf, because he has received him back safe and healthy.’
But he was angry, and would not go in. Therefore his father came out, and begged him.
But he answered his father, ‘Behold, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed a commandment of yours, but you never gave me a goat, that I might celebrate with my friends.
But when this your son came, who has devoured your living with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him.’
“He said to him, ‘Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours.
But it was appropriate to celebrate and be glad, for this, your brother, was dead, and is alive again. He was lost, and is found.’ ”
b: In this passage Jesus continues the parable of the prodigal son, this time focusing on the elder son's reaction. The elder son is angry and resentful that the father celebrates the prodigal's return, because he thinks he has served his father faithfully yet never been treated like this. This passage deeply exposes the jealousy and self-righteousness in the human heart, and reminds us that God's love is unconditional and beyond our understanding.

Jesus' parable tells us that even if we seem faithful outwardly, we may be full of jealousy and resentment deep inside. The elder son could not understand his father's love and forgiveness because he valued merit and reward rather than the father's grace and mercy. This reminds us to guard our hearts at all times, making sure we do not measure others by self-righteousness, but treat them with God's eyes and heart.

Through this passage God tells us that his love and grace are unconditional; whatever our past, when we return to him he opens his arms to receive us. We should learn God's love and forgiveness, being faithful not only in conduct but also in heart, aligned with God's heart.
q: Are there times in your life when jealousy and self-righteousness have made you resentful? How can you learn God's love and forgiveness in treating others?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for your boundless grace and love, which help us understand that your love goes beyond merit and performance. Help us to remove jealousy and self-righteousness from our hearts, to treat others with forgiveness and love, and to see this world with your heart. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: He also said to his disciples, “There was a certain rich man who had a manager. An accusation was made to him that this man was wasting his possessions.
He called him, and said to him, ‘What is this that I hear about you? Give an accounting of your management, for you can no longer be manager.’
“The manager said within himself, ‘What will I do, seeing that my lord is taking away the management position from me? I don’t have strength to dig. I am ashamed to beg.
I know what I will do, so that when I am removed from management, they may receive me into their houses.’
Calling each one of his lord’s debtors to him, he said to the first, ‘How much do you owe to my lord?’
He said, ‘A hundred batos of oil.’ He said to him, ‘Take your bill, and sit down quickly and write fifty.’
Then he said to another, ‘How much do you owe?’ He said, ‘A hundred cors of wheat.’ He said to him, ‘Take your bill, and write eighty.’
“His lord commended the dishonest manager because he had done wisely, for the children of this world are, in their own generation, wiser than the children of the light.
I tell you, make for yourselves friends by means of unrighteous mammon, so that when you fail, they may receive you into the eternal tents.
b: In this passage Jesus uses the parable of the dishonest manager to teach us to use resources wisely. Facing the crisis of losing his job, the manager quickly thinks of reducing people's debts to prepare for his future. Although his method is immoral, his shrewdness and prompt action are praised by his master. Through this Jesus reminds us to handle the things of this life, especially money, wisely, in preparation for the life to come.

Jesus' parable is not praising dishonesty, but stressing that as "children of light," we should be even shrewder and more active in spiritual matters. We should use the resources God gives us wisely, not only for the needs of this life but for eternal value. We need to ask ourselves whether we are wisely managing and using everything God has entrusted to us, and preparing for the life to come.

Through this passage God tells us that he wants us to be wise and good stewards, excelling not only in the affairs of this life but acting actively in spiritual matters. We should always remember that everything in this life prepares for the life to come, and manage our resources with an eternal perspective.
q: In your daily life, are you wisely managing the resources God has entrusted to you? How can you prepare more for eternity and use these resources to glorify God?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for teaching us how to use the resources of this life wisely. Help us to be faithful and shrewd stewards, living for eternal values and not focusing only on the needs of this life. May all our actions glorify you and store up treasure for the life to come. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much. He who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much.
If therefore you have not been faithful in the unrighteous mammon, who will commit to your trust the true riches?
If you have not been faithful in that which is another’s, who will give you that which is your own?
No servant can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to one, and despise the other. You aren’t able to serve God and Mammon.”
b: In this passage Jesus teaches us principles of faithfulness and service. He stresses that in daily life we should show our faithfulness even in the smallest matters. This passage reminds us that how we handle finances and material things is an important test of our spiritual life. Jesus points out that if we are not faithful with these temporary possessions, we cannot be entrusted with greater spiritual responsibility.

Jesus also points out that no one can serve two masters, referring especially to the choice between money and God. He warns us that the pursuit of wealth may lead us away from God and bind our hearts to worldly pursuits. We must choose to give our hearts and lives wholly to God, rather than be tempted and ruled by material things.

Through this passage God tells us that faithfulness and singleness of heart are the basic requirements for serving him. We should ask ourselves whether we show faithfulness to God in everything and give him our whole heart. God calls us to manage everything he has given us faithfully, whether material possessions or spiritual gifts.
q: In your daily life, are you faithful in managing material things and finances? How can you serve God more singlemindedly and not be led by worldly temptations?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for reminding us of the importance of faithfulness and singleness of heart. Help us to show faithfulness to you in everything and to serve you with undivided hearts. May we not be bound by the pursuit of material things in daily life, but serve you with all our hearts. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: The Pharisees, who were lovers of money, also heard all these things, and they scoffed at him.
He said to them, “You are those who justify yourselves in the sight of men, but God knows your hearts. For that which is exalted among men is an abomination in the sight of God.
b: In this passage Jesus directly challenges the attitude of the Pharisees, especially their love of money. The Pharisees displayed their righteousness through outward piety and legal observance, but Jesus points out that God looks at the heart, not at outward conduct. Jesus exposes the greed in their hearts and stresses that piety displayed before people may be worthless before God.

Jesus' words remind us that outward religious activity cannot please God; what he values are the motives and attitudes of our hearts. This passage challenges us to ask whether we, like the Pharisees, focus only on outward righteousness and neglect our true inner state. God calls our lives to be sincere, inside and out, aimed at pleasing him and not at winning human praise.

Through this passage God tells us that he cares about our inner motives, not only our outward conduct. We should ask ourselves whether we are like the Pharisees, overvaluing appearance and neglecting purity of heart. God calls us to serve him with a sincere heart, and to let our actions be consistent with our faith.
q: In your relationship with God, do you sometimes focus too much on outward appearance and neglect purity of heart? How can you better keep your heart sincere and pure in daily life?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for reminding us of the importance of the heart. Help us to be sincere and pure before you. May we not merely do good outwardly, but truly serve you with a pure heart. May our lives, inside and out, display your glory and please you. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: The law and the prophets were until John. From that time the Good News of God’s Kingdom is preached, and everyone is forcing his way into it.
But it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away, than for one tiny stroke of a pen in the law to fall.
Everyone who divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery. He who marries one who is divorced from a husband commits adultery.
b: In this passage Jesus stresses the importance of the law and declares that the gospel of God's kingdom has begun to spread. He points out that the law and the prophets were until John, and from then on the good news of the kingdom is preached. Jesus also warns that although the gospel is spreading, the law is still valid and requires strict observance.

Jesus especially mentions the sanctity of marriage, stressing that divorcing one's wife and marrying another is adultery. This reminds us that God takes marriage seriously, and we should treat the vows of marriage with reverence. This passage calls us to re-examine our attitude toward God's law and marriage vows, making sure our conduct accords with God's will.

Through this passage God tells us that his law does not change; however the times change, God's standard remains. We should take God's word seriously and put these teachings into practice in life, especially in marriage and family relationships, showing loyalty and reverence toward God.
q: In your relationship with God, are you faithful in keeping his law, especially in marriage and family relationships? How can you better put God's teachings into practice in daily life?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for giving us the law and the gospel to help us understand your will. Give us strength to follow your teachings strictly in life, especially in marriage and family relationships. May all our conduct glorify you and show loyalty and reverence toward you. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: “Now there was a certain rich man, and he was clothed in purple and fine linen, living in luxury every day.
A certain beggar, named Lazarus, was taken to his gate, full of sores,
and desiring to be fed with the crumbs that fell from the rich man’s table. Yes, even the dogs came and licked his sores.
The beggar died, and he was carried away by the angels to Abraham’s bosom. The rich man also died, and was buried.
In Hades, he lifted up his eyes, being in torment, and saw Abraham far off, and Lazarus at his bosom.
He cried and said, ‘Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus, that he may dip the tip of his finger in water, and cool my tongue! For I am in anguish in this flame.’
“But Abraham said, ‘Son, remember that you, in your lifetime, received your good things, and Lazarus, in the same way, bad things. But here he is now comforted, and you are in anguish.
Besides all this, between us and you there is a great gulf fixed, that those who want to pass from here to you are not able, and that no one may cross over from there to us.’
“He said, ‘I ask you therefore, father, that you would send him to my father’s house;
for I have five brothers, that he may testify to them, so they won’t also come into this place of torment.’
“But Abraham said to him, ‘They have Moses and the prophets. Let them listen to them.’
“He said, ‘No, father Abraham, but if one goes to them from the dead, they will repent.’
“He said to him, ‘If they don’t listen to Moses and the prophets, neither will they be persuaded if one rises from the dead.’ ”
b: In this passage Jesus, through the parable of the rich man and Lazarus, teaches us a solemn truth about eternal life. The rich man lives in luxury in this life, while Lazarus lives in poverty and suffering. But after death their fates are completely reversed: Lazarus is carried to Abraham's side and comforted, while the rich man is in torment in Hades. This reminds us that wealth and status in this life do not guarantee eternal happiness; true blessing lies in our relationship with God.

In his torment the rich man begs Abraham to send Lazarus to warn his brothers, but Abraham replies that they have Moses and the prophets to listen to; if they do not listen to them, they will not repent even if someone rises from the dead. This warns us not to treat God's word lightly, because God has already made his will known to us through Scripture.

Through this passage God tells us that our choices in this life determine our eternal destiny. We should listen carefully to God's word and obey it, and not be deceived by the material temptations and pleasures of this life. This passage calls us to examine whether our way of life now accords with God's will, and to make the right choices for eternal life.
q: In your daily life, are you tempted by the material things and pleasures of this life? How can you live more with an eternal perspective and obey God's word?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for reminding us of the truth of life through Jesus' parable. Help us not to be deceived by the material things of this life, but to live with an eternal perspective. May we make the right choices in this life and obey your word, preparing ourselves for eternal life. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: He said to the disciples, “It is impossible that no occasions of stumbling should come, but woe to him through whom they come!
It would be better for him if a millstone were hung around his neck, and he were thrown into the sea, rather than that he should cause one of these little ones to stumble.
Be careful. If your brother sins against you, rebuke him. If he repents, forgive him.
If he sins against you seven times in the day, and seven times returns, saying, ‘I repent,’ you shall forgive him.”
b: In this passage Jesus reminds us that stumbling blocks are bound to come in this world, but those who become stumbling blocks to others will bear serious consequences. Jesus uses a stern picture, saying that it would be better for anyone who causes "one of these little ones" to stumble to have a millstone hung around his neck and be thrown into the sea. This stresses how seriously we should take our influence on the spiritual lives of others, especially those whose faith is not yet mature.

Jesus then teaches us how to treat our brothers and sisters: when a brother sins against us, we should rebuke him, and forgive him when he repents. This passage especially stresses the importance of forgiveness; even if we are wronged seven times in a day, we should still be willing to forgive. This continual readiness to forgive reflects God's mercy and forgiveness toward us, and we should treat others with the same heart.

Through this passage God tells us that our conduct has a deep influence on others, so we should be careful in word and deed and not become stumbling blocks. We should also learn the lesson of forgiveness, because it is what God requires of us. We should ask ourselves whether we are willing to forgive unconditionally those who wrong us, and put this forgiving love into practice.
q: In your life, have you ever become a stumbling block to others through your words or actions? How can you forgive others more in daily life and avoid becoming an obstacle to their spiritual growth?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for teaching us the lesson of forgiveness. Help us not to become stumbling blocks to others, and to learn to forgive others unconditionally. May our words and deeds glorify you and help others grow spiritually. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: The apostles said to the Lord, “Increase our faith.”
The Lord said, “If you had faith like a grain of mustard seed, you would tell this sycamore tree, ‘Be uprooted, and be planted in the sea,’ and it would obey you.
b: In this passage the apostles ask Jesus to increase their faith. Jesus' reply stresses the power of faith: even faith as small as a mustard seed can have great effect. With this picture Jesus tells us that faith is not a matter of its size, but of how we use it to trust God's power and promises.

Jesus says that if we have faith, we can say to a mulberry tree, "Be uprooted and planted in the sea," and it will obey us. This powerful image reminds us that true faith goes beyond the limits of the natural world and can witness God's mighty power. Jesus' teaching encourages us to exercise faith in every area of life, trusting God's will and work even in situations that seem impossible.

Through this passage God tells us that faith is the foundation of our spiritual life. We do not need great faith, only a real and continuing trust in God's word and power. We should ask whether we are truly exercising faith in life and trusting that God can fulfill his promises. When we learn to act by faith, we will witness God's wonderful work in our lives.
q: In your daily life, do you have enough faith to face challenges? How can you better exercise faith to witness God's power and work?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for the gift of faith. Help us to exercise this faith in life, and whatever the circumstances, to trust your power and promises. May our faith witness your work and bring spiritual breakthrough. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: But who is there among you, having a servant plowing or keeping sheep, that will say when he comes in from the field, ‘Come immediately and sit down at the table,’
and will not rather tell him, ‘Prepare my supper, clothe yourself properly, and serve me, while I eat and drink. Afterward you shall eat and drink’?
Does he thank that servant because he did the things that were commanded? I think not.
Even so you also, when you have done all the things that are commanded you, say, ‘We are unworthy servants. We have done our duty.’ ”
b: In this passage Jesus teaches us the humble attitude a servant should have. He uses a simple picture to describe the relationship between master and servant. When the servant has finished his work, the master does not thank him specially, because it was his duty. In the same way, Jesus reminds us that when we have done the work God has entrusted to us, we should keep a humble attitude, knowing we have only done what we ought.

Jesus' teaching challenges us to examine our attitude in service. When we serve in God's kingdom, do we expect human praise and thanks? Or can we simply serve the Lord faithfully with a servant's heart, whether or not we receive anything in return? This passage calls us to stay humble and obedient in serving God, and not to be proud of the good we have done.

Through this passage God tells us that serving him is an honor and also our duty. We should ask ourselves whether we have a humble heart in service, and remember that everything we do is to glorify God, not to receive human praise or reward. May we serve faithfully in God's kingdom and walk the spiritual path with a servant's heart.
q: As you serve God, do you keep a humble heart? How can you better glorify God in service without seeking human praise or reward?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for calling us to serve in your kingdom. Give us a humble heart, so that in service we do not seek human praise but act solely to glorify you. May our lives be a witness to your glory and faithfully fulfill the mission you have entrusted to us. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: As he was on his way to Jerusalem, he was passing along the borders of Samaria and Galilee.
As he entered into a certain village, ten men who were lepers met him, who stood at a distance.
They lifted up their voices, saying, “Jesus, Master, have mercy on us!”
When he saw them, he said to them, “Go and show yourselves to the priests.” As they went, they were cleansed.
One of them, when he saw that he was healed, turned back, glorifying God with a loud voice.
He fell on his face at Jesus’ feet, giving him thanks; and he was a Samaritan.
Jesus answered, “Weren’t the ten cleansed? But where are the nine?
Were there none found who returned to give glory to God, except this foreigner?”
Then he said to him, “Get up, and go your way. Your faith has healed you.”
b: In this passage, as Jesus passes through a village, he meets ten men with leprosy. They stand at a distance and cry out for Jesus to have mercy on them. Jesus sees their suffering and tells them to go and show themselves to the priests, and on the way they are cleansed. But only one comes back to thank Jesus, and he is a Samaritan. Jesus is amazed at this and commends the faith of this foreigner.

This passage reminds us to ask whether, like the nine who were cleansed, we forget to be thankful. When we experience God's grace and healing, do we remember to return to him and thank him for his blessings? The Samaritan's thankful heart should be our example: whatever grace we receive, we should first give glory to God.

Through this passage God tells us that a thankful heart is an indispensable part of the Christian life. We should often ask ourselves whether, after receiving God's blessings, we remember to thank him. Thankfulness is the right response to God's grace; it keeps us humble and helps us experience God's love and grace more deeply.
q: When you experience God's grace and blessings, do you remember to thank him? How can you better keep a thankful heart in daily life?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for the countless times you have given us grace and healing. Help us to keep a thankful heart always and to remember to give glory to you. May our lives be a witness of thanksgiving, drawing closer to you with every experience. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: Being asked by the Pharisees when God’s Kingdom would come, he answered them, “God’s Kingdom doesn’t come with observation;
neither will they say, ‘Look, here!’ or, ‘Look, there!’ for behold, God’s Kingdom is within you.”
b: In this passage the Pharisees ask Jesus when the kingdom of God will come. Jesus' answer surprises them: he says the kingdom of God does not come with observation, because the kingdom of God is within you. This reveals the spiritual nature of God's kingdom; it is not limited to a geographic location or a physical phenomenon, but exists in the hearts of those who accept and obey God.

Jesus' answer reminds us that God's kingdom is invisible, yet it truly works in the heart of every believer. This passage challenges us to ask whether we truly understand and experience the presence of God's kingdom in our lives. God's kingdom is expressed in believers' lives as righteousness, peace, and joy, and is at the core of our inner life.

Through this passage God tells us that God's kingdom is not a future event or an external phenomenon, but a real spiritual experience. When we let God rule our hearts and lives, God's kingdom is realized within us. This calls us to welcome God's kingdom every day with obedience and faith, and to show his glory in our lives.
q: Do you sense God's kingdom working in your heart in daily life? How can you let God rule your life more and show his kingdom in your life?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for giving us your kingdom. Help us to experience and show your kingdom in daily life. May our hearts be the place of your kingdom, bearing witness to your presence with righteousness, peace, and joy. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: He said to the disciples, “The days will come when you will desire to see one of the days of the Son of Man, and you will not see it.
They will tell you, ‘Look, here!’ or ‘Look, there!’ Don’t go away or follow after them,
for as the lightning, when it flashes out of one part under the sky, shines to another part under the sky; so will the Son of Man be in his day.
But first, he must suffer many things and be rejected by this generation.
b: In this passage Jesus warns his disciples that a day will come when they will long to see one of the days of the Son of Man, but will not see it. Jesus reminds them not to be misled by those who claim to have seen the Son of Man, because when Jesus returns it will be as plain as lightning, and no one can miss it. Before his glorious return, however, Jesus must first suffer and be rejected.

This passage reminds us that Jesus' return will be a public, undeniable event, and we should wait patiently for that day rather than be misled by rumors and false prophecies. Jesus also teaches that those who follow him must be ready to face the hostility and trials of this generation, because he himself must go through suffering and rejection.

Through this passage God tells us that we should stay alert and patient as we wait for Jesus' return, and also be prepared to face the challenges and trials of this world. We can be sure that when that day comes God's kingdom will be fully realized, all suffering will end, and we will share glory with the Lord.
q: As you wait for Jesus' return, are you keeping faith and staying alert? How can you stand firm when facing trials and challenges?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for the promise of Jesus' return. Help us to keep faith and stay alert as we wait. May we not be misled by the temptations of the world, but follow you steadfastly and be ready to face any challenge. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: As it was in the days of Noah, even so will it be also in the days of the Son of Man.
They ate, they drank, they married, and they were given in marriage until the day that Noah entered into the ship, and the flood came and destroyed them all.
Likewise, even as it was in the days of Lot: they ate, they drank, they bought, they sold, they planted, they built;
but in the day that Lot went out from Sodom, it rained fire and sulfur from the sky and destroyed them all.
It will be the same way in the day that the Son of Man is revealed.
b: In this passage Jesus uses the days of Noah and Lot as examples to warn us that when he returns, people may still be living as usual, ignoring the coming judgment. In the days of Noah and of Lot, though people were absorbed in daily activities, judgment came suddenly, and only Noah and Lot were saved because they obeyed God.

This passage reminds us that Jesus' return will come as suddenly as that judgment, so we must be ready at all times. This readiness is not only a change of outward conduct but an inner reverence and obedience toward God. We should ask ourselves whether we truly realize how important all this is, and live out in daily life a life that matches this hope.

Through this passage God tells us that Jesus' return is certain, and the way we live now will determine whether we are ready to face his coming. God calls us to live in his light, to leave every way of life that does not please him, and to hold fast to faith until that day comes.
q: In your daily life, are you aware of the urgency of Jesus' return? How can you better prepare yourself to welcome that glorious day?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for reminding us of the day of Jesus' return. Help us to stay alert and be ready to welcome that day. May our lives reflect reverence and obedience toward you, and bear witness to your kingdom in this generation. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: In that day, he who will be on the housetop and his goods in the house, let him not go down to take them away. Let him who is in the field likewise not turn back.
Remember Lot’s wife!
Whoever seeks to save his life loses it, but whoever loses his life preserves it.
I tell you, in that night there will be two people in one bed. One will be taken and the other will be left.
There will be two grinding grain together. One will be taken and the other will be left.”
They, answering, asked him, “Where, Lord?” He said to them, “Where the body is, there the vultures will also be gathered together.”
b: In this passage Jesus warns us to be ready for his return, and tells us to remember Lot's wife. Lot's wife lost her life because she looked back at Sodom; this tells us that in the face of God's judgment we should not cling to worldly things, but focus on God's kingdom. Jesus goes on to stress that when he returns there will be a separation: one taken, the other left.

This passage reminds us that in facing the judgment of the last days, obedience and loyalty to God are the key. We should ask ourselves whether we, like Lot's wife, are attached to worldly things, or have a heart focused on God's kingdom. Jesus' teaching calls us, whatever the circumstances, to hold fast to our faith and not be weighed down by the temptations of the world.

Through this passage God tells us that his judgment will bring a clear separation, and the choices we make now will determine our destiny. God calls us to let go of our attachment to this present age, focus on eternal values, stay firm in faith, and welcome his return.
q: In your daily life, are you still attached to worldly things? How can you focus better on God's kingdom and prepare yourself to welcome the Lord's return?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for reminding us of the urgency of Jesus' return. Help us to let go of our attachment to this present age and focus on your kingdom. May we stay firm in faith in this generation and be ready to welcome your return. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: He also spoke a parable to them that they must always pray, and not give up,
saying, “There was a judge in a certain city who didn’t fear God, and didn’t respect man.
A widow was in that city, and she often came to him, saying, ‘Defend me from my adversary!’
He wouldn’t for a while, but afterward he said to himself, ‘Though I neither fear God, nor respect man,
yet because this widow bothers me, I will defend her, or else she will wear me out by her continual coming.’ ”
The Lord said, “Listen to what the unrighteous judge says.
Won’t God avenge his chosen ones who are crying out to him day and night, and yet he exercises patience with them?
I tell you that he will avenge them quickly. Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on the earth?”
b: In this passage Jesus uses a parable to teach us to pray always and not lose heart. The widow in the story had long been oppressed by an unrighteous man, and she kept appealing to a judge who did not fear God, until, because of her persistence, he was compelled to give her justice. Through this parable Jesus tells us that although it may sometimes seem that God has not answered our prayers right away, we should not lose faith because of it.

Jesus' teaching reminds us that prayer is more than telling God what we need; it is an expression of our faith. Our persistence and patience reflect our trust in God. Even in situations that look hopeless we should keep on praying, because God will surely hear and answer our cry.

Through this passage God tells us that he is faithful and will answer our prayers in his own time. He longs to see our faith, and he wants us to show our trust in him as we pray. Let us persevere in prayer, confident that God's purpose will be fulfilled in our lives.
q: When you face hardship, do you easily lose heart while waiting? How can you stay persistent in prayer and trust God's timing and plans?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for the privilege of prayer. Help us hold on to faith in times of hardship and not lose heart while we wait. May we keep seeking your will in prayer, and believe that you will surely bring about your good plan in our lives. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: He spoke also this parable to certain people who were convinced of their own righteousness, and who despised all others.
“Two men went up into the temple to pray; one was a Pharisee, and the other was a tax collector.
The Pharisee stood and prayed to himself like this: ‘God, I thank you that I am not like the rest of men, extortionists, unrighteous, adulterers, or even like this tax collector.
I fast twice a week. I give tithes of all that I get.’
But the tax collector, standing far away, wouldn’t even lift up his eyes to heaven, but beat his breast, saying, ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner!’
I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other; for everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but he who humbles himself will be exalted.”
b: In this passage Jesus uses the parable of the Pharisee and the tax collector to teach us about true humility. The Pharisee considered himself righteous, proudly listed his good deeds, and looked down on the tax collector. The tax collector, by contrast, recognized his sin and humbly begged for God's mercy. Jesus says that in the end it was the humble tax collector who went home justified before God, not the self-righteous Pharisee.

Jesus' parable reminds us that true righteousness comes not from our works but from humility before God and dependence on him. What God values is the attitude of our hearts, not our outward performance. When we recognize our weakness and our lack, and repent sincerely, God's mercy comes to us.

Through this passage God tells us that he opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble. We should reflect on whether we have become proud in our faith, or lacking in compassion for the weaknesses of others. May we remain humble before God and always recognize that we need his grace and mercy.
q: In your life of faith, have you ever become proud because of your own righteous deeds? How can you stay humble and admit your shortcomings before God?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for your mercy and grace. Help us stay humble before you and not become proud because of what we have done. Make us always aware of our shortcomings, and give us compassion for those who need your grace. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: They were also bringing their babies to him, that he might touch them. But when the disciples saw it, they rebuked them.
Jesus summoned them, saying, “Allow the little children to come to me, and don’t hinder them, for God’s Kingdom belongs to such as these.
Most certainly, I tell you, whoever doesn’t receive God’s Kingdom like a little child, he will in no way enter into it.”
b: In this passage Jesus emphasizes the place of little children in the kingdom of God. The disciples thought children were unimportant and tried to keep them from coming to Jesus, but Jesus corrected them, saying that the kingdom of God belongs to such as these. He went on to teach that whoever wants to enter God's kingdom must come with the purity, humility and trust of a little child.

Jesus' teaching reminds us that entering God's kingdom has nothing to do with status or achievement, but with whether we have the purity and simple trust of a child. A child has no complicated schemes and does not rely on his own strength; he trusts his parents completely, and this is exactly how we should relate to God. We need to depend simply on God's grace, like children, rather than on our own ability.

Through this passage God tells us that what he values is a simple heart and trust in him. The kingdom of God is not prepared for the proud and self-reliant, but for those who are willing to put self aside and depend entirely on God. May we learn to keep a pure and humble heart before God, like a little child.
q: On your journey of faith, can you be pure and trusting like a child? Is there any part of your life where you need to depend more deeply on God rather than on your own ability?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for welcoming us with unconditional love. Help us keep a childlike purity and trust before you. Make us willing to lay self aside and learn to depend entirely on your grace rather than on our own strength. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: A certain ruler asked him, saying, “Good Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?”
Jesus asked him, “Why do you call me good? No one is good, except one: God.
You know the commandments: ‘Don’t commit adultery,’ ‘Don’t murder,’ ‘Don’t steal,’ ‘Don’t give false testimony,’ ‘Honor your father and your mother.’ ”
He said, “I have observed all these things from my youth up.”
When Jesus heard these things, he said to him, “You still lack one thing. Sell all that you have, and distribute it to the poor. Then you will have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me.”
But when he heard these things, he became very sad, for he was very rich.
b: In this passage a rich ruler comes to Jesus asking how to inherit eternal life. The ruler confidently declares that he has kept the commandments since his youth, but Jesus points out what his heart still lacks: he is to sell all that he has, give to the poor, and then follow Jesus. But the ruler became very sad because of his wealth, and in the end he could not follow Jesus.

Jesus' response exposes the ruler's heart problem: although he kept the commandments, his heart was bound by riches, and he could not give himself fully to follow Jesus. This passage reminds us that having wealth or position is not itself a sin; the real challenge is whether our hearts cling to these worldly possessions so that we cannot trust and follow God wholeheartedly.

Through this passage God tells us that he wants more than outward obedience to the law; he wants us to let go of our attachment to material things and follow his call. The kingdom of God is prepared for those who are willing to leave everything behind and follow Jesus without condition. May we reflect on our dependence on material things, and learn to entrust everything in our hearts to God and follow him fully.
q: In your life, are material things keeping you from following God wholeheartedly? How can you let go of your attachment to possessions and learn to entrust everything to God?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for reminding us not to let material things bind our hearts. Help us let go of our attachment to wealth and learn to follow you with all our heart. Make us able to place our lives in your hands without reservation and follow your will. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: Jesus, seeing that he became very sad, said, “How hard it is for those who have riches to enter into God’s Kingdom!
For it is easier for a camel to enter in through a needle’s eye than for a rich man to enter into God’s Kingdom.”
Those who heard it said, “Then who can be saved?”
But he said, “The things which are impossible with men are possible with God.”
b: In this passage, after the rich ruler walks away, Jesus gives his disciples a sobering warning: "How hard it is for those who have riches to enter into the Kingdom of God!"
