These words reveal the power of wealth to bind the heart, so that it often becomes hard for people to depend wholly on God. Jesus went on to say that it is easier for a camel to go through a needle's eye than for a rich man to enter God's kingdom, and his hearers were astonished.

Jesus' teaching reminds us that having wealth is not in itself a sin, but it can become an obstacle to our spiritual growth. Wealth easily leads people to rely too much on their own ability and to neglect trusting God. Jesus stresses that by our own strength it is nearly impossible to enter God's kingdom, but with God all things are possible.

Through this passage God tells us that our salvation does not depend on ourselves but on God's grace and power. Even obstacles that seem impossible to us, God can help us overcome. Let us learn to entrust our lives completely to God, believing that he is able to lead us into his kingdom.
q: In your life, do wealth or other material things make you feel spiritually hindered? How can you depend on God more deeply and rise above these obstacles?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for reminding us not to depend on wealth but to rely on you with all our heart. Help us let go of our attachment to material things and learn to depend on your grace to enter your kingdom. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: Peter said, “Look, we have left everything and followed you.”
He said to them, “Most certainly I tell you, there is no one who has left house, or wife, or brothers, or parents, or children, for God’s Kingdom’s sake,
who will not receive many times more in this time, and in the world to come, eternal life.”
b: In this passage Peter says that he and the other disciples have left everything to follow Jesus. Jesus answers Peter by assuring him that everyone who has left worldly possessions or relationships for the sake of God's kingdom will receive many times more in this present time, and in the age to come, eternal life. This is Jesus' affirmation and encouragement of the disciples' sacrifice, and a promise to every Christian.

Jesus' teaching reminds us that following him may require giving up some things in this world, but he promises that such sacrifice will not be in vain. God will bless us in different ways in this life, and more importantly, will give us eternal life in the age to come. This passage encourages us not to hesitate over letting go of worldly things, because God's reward far exceeds anything we can imagine.

Through this passage God tells us that he watches over those who make sacrifices for his kingdom. Whatever we give for him, he will answer with blessings many times over. We should follow him with confidence, knowing that what we give has infinite value in God's eyes.
q: In your life, have you had to give something up in order to follow God's call? How can you find peace and joy in those sacrifices, trusting that God's blessing far exceeds what you have given?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for promising that the sacrifices we make for your kingdom will not be in vain. Give us courage and faith to let go of everything in this world and follow you wholeheartedly, trusting in your blessings and promises. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: He took the twelve aside, and said to them, “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and all the things that are written through the prophets concerning the Son of Man will be completed.
For he will be delivered up to the Gentiles, will be mocked, treated shamefully, and spit on.
They will scourge and kill him. On the third day, he will rise again.”
They understood none of these things. This saying was hidden from them, and they didn’t understand the things that were said.
b: In this passage Jesus foretells his suffering in Jerusalem. He tells his disciples plainly that he will be handed over to the Gentiles, mocked, shamefully treated, flogged and killed, but that on the third day he will rise again. Yet the disciples could not understand his words and were confused by these predictions.

Jesus' prophecy shows that he clearly understood and accepted the suffering that lay ahead. He knew his mission and was willing to endure all suffering for the redemption of humankind. This passage reminds us that Jesus' suffering was no accident but part of God's plan of redemption, and that his resurrection brings the hope of eternal life.

Through this passage God tells us that Jesus' sacrifice and resurrection are the heart of our faith. We may not fully understand God's plan, just as the disciples did not understand then, but we can trust God's wisdom and grace. Jesus has paid the highest price for us, and we should respond to his love with grateful hearts.
q: What does it mean for your faith that Jesus suffered and rose again for you? In daily life, how do you practically express your thanks for Jesus' sacrifice?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for giving us Jesus Christ, who suffered for us and rose again so that we could be reconciled to you. Help us understand and treasure Jesus' sacrifice more in our daily lives, and respond to his love with grateful hearts. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: As he came near Jericho, a certain blind man sat by the road, begging.
Hearing a multitude going by, he asked what this meant.
They told him that Jesus of Nazareth was passing by.
He cried out, “Jesus, you son of David, have mercy on me!”
Those who led the way rebuked him, that he should be quiet; but he cried out all the more, “You son of David, have mercy on me!”
Standing still, Jesus commanded him to be brought to him. When he had come near, he asked him,
“What do you want me to do?” He said, “Lord, that I may see again.”
Jesus said to him, “Receive your sight. Your faith has healed you.”
Immediately he received his sight and followed him, glorifying God. All the people, when they saw it, praised God.
b: In this passage a blind man hears that Jesus is passing by. Though he cannot see, he is full of faith and cries out loudly for Jesus' mercy. Although the crowd tried to silence him, he cried out all the more. When Jesus heard him, he stopped and asked what he wanted, and the blind man said he wanted to receive his sight. Jesus praised his faith and healed him at once, and he could see.

The blind man's actions show his great faith in Jesus. Even though the crowd rebuked him and tried to stop him, he never gave up calling for Jesus' mercy. Jesus responded to his faith by healing his eyes so that he could see. This passage reminds us that faith is vital before God: however difficult our situation, if we firmly trust God's power and mercy, he will answer our prayers.

Through this passage God tells us that he hears those who come with faith and longing. We should learn from this blind man's example: whatever difficulty we meet, we should trust God firmly, believe in his power and love, and boldly cry out to him for help.
q: When you face difficulties, do you call on God for help as steadfastly as the blind man did? How can you depend on God more deeply in life and believe that he will answer your prayers?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for hearing our prayers and healing the weakness of our hearts and bodies. Increase our faith, so that in hard times we may rely firmly on you and believe in your power and mercy. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: He entered and was passing through Jericho.
There was a man named Zacchaeus. He was a chief tax collector, and he was rich.
He was trying to see who Jesus was, and couldn’t because of the crowd, because he was short.
He ran on ahead, and climbed up into a sycamore tree to see him, for he was going to pass that way.
When Jesus came to the place, he looked up and saw him, and said to him, “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for today I must stay at your house.”
He hurried, came down, and received him joyfully.
When they saw it, they all murmured, saying, “He has gone in to lodge with a man who is a sinner.”
Zacchaeus stood and said to the Lord, “Behold, Lord, half of my goods I give to the poor. If I have wrongfully exacted anything of anyone, I restore four times as much.”
Jesus said to him, “Today, salvation has come to this house, because he also is a son of Abraham.
For the Son of Man came to seek and to save that which was lost.”
b: In this passage Zacchaeus is a chief tax collector, regarded by society as a sinner. Although he was wealthy, his heart longed to know Jesus. Because he was short, he ran ahead and climbed a sycamore tree to see Jesus. Jesus noticed what he did and took the initiative to invite himself to Zacchaeus' house. Moved by this grace, Zacchaeus decided to repent and said he would make amends for his past wrongs with real actions.

Jesus' action shows the purpose for which he came into the world: to seek and to save that which was lost. Zacchaeus' story tells us that whatever our past, if we are willing to repent and believe in Jesus, he will receive us and bring us salvation. Zacchaeus' change also shows the fruit of true repentance: being willing to pay the price for one's wrongs and actively doing good.

Through this passage God tells us that he unconditionally welcomes every sinner who is willing to repent. However dark our past may be, Jesus' love can change us and make us new creations. Let us learn from Zacchaeus' example: when we meet Jesus, may we be willing to change our lives completely and live out the fruit of repentance.
q: Zacchaeus' repentance brought a change of life. After meeting Jesus, are you willing to change your life completely? In what areas do you need to show actions of repentance as Zacchaeus did?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for sending Jesus to seek and save us who were lost. May our lives be changed by Jesus' love and bear the fruit of repentance, to the glory of your name. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: As they heard these things, he went on and told a parable, because he was near Jerusalem, and they supposed that God’s Kingdom would be revealed immediately.
He said therefore, “A certain nobleman went into a far country to receive for himself a kingdom and to return.
He called ten servants of his and gave them ten mina coins,  and told them, ‘Conduct business until I come.’
But his citizens hated him, and sent an envoy after him, saying, ‘We don’t want this man to reign over us.’

“When he had come back again, having received the kingdom, he commanded these servants, to whom he had given the money, to be called to him, that he might know what they had gained by conducting business.
The first came before him, saying, ‘Lord, your mina has made ten more minas.’
“He said to him, ‘Well done, you good servant! Because you were found faithful with very little, you shall have authority over ten cities.’
“The second came, saying, ‘Your mina, Lord, has made five minas.’
“So he said to him, ‘And you are to be over five cities.’
Another came, saying, ‘Lord, behold, your mina, which I kept laid away in a handkerchief,
for I feared you, because you are an exacting man. You take up that which you didn’t lay down, and reap that which you didn’t sow.’
“He said to him, ‘Out of your own mouth I will judge you, you wicked servant! You knew that I am an exacting man, taking up that which I didn’t lay down, and reaping that which I didn’t sow.
Then why didn’t you deposit my money in the bank, and at my coming, I might have earned interest on it?’
He said to those who stood by, ‘Take the mina away from him and give it to him who has the ten minas.’
“They said to him, ‘Lord, he has ten minas!’
‘For I tell you that to everyone who has, will more be given; but from him who doesn’t have, even that which he has will be taken away from him.
But bring those enemies of mine who didn’t want me to reign over them here, and kill them before me.’ ”
b: In this passage Jesus tells a parable about faithfulness and responsibility. The nobleman in the parable represents Jesus himself: he leaves this world but will finally return, and he will judge each person's faithfulness and conduct. The servants who faithfully managed their master's goods received greater rewards, while the servant who did nothing out of fear lost everything he had.

Jesus' parable reminds us that each person has been given different talents and responsibilities, and we must faithfully manage these resources and work for God's kingdom. This passage stresses the importance of action: faith alone is not enough; we must turn our faith into concrete deeds and actively respond to God's call.

Through this passage God tells us that one day he will examine how we have used everything he has given us. Are we serving God faithfully in our place? Are we making good use of the resources he has given us to contribute to his kingdom? Let us face every opportunity God gives us with faithfulness, and look forward to receiving his praise when the Lord returns.
q: In your life, are you faithfully managing everything God has given you? How can you make better use of your talents and resources to contribute to God's kingdom?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for giving us different talents and opportunities. Help us manage all of it faithfully and respond to your call with action. Make us able to serve you faithfully every day as we look forward to your return. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: Having said these things, he went on ahead, going up to Jerusalem.
When he came near to Bethsphage and Bethany, at the mountain that is called Olivet, he sent two of his disciples,
saying, “Go your way into the village on the other side, in which, as you enter, you will find a colt tied, which no man had ever sat upon. Untie it and bring it.
If anyone asks you, ‘Why are you untying it?’ say to him: ‘The Lord needs it.’ ”
Those who were sent went away, and found things just as he had told them.
As they were untying the colt, its owners said to them, “Why are you untying the colt?”
They said, “The Lord needs it.”
Then they brought it to Jesus. They threw their cloaks on the colt, and sat Jesus on them.
As he went, they spread their cloaks on the road.
As he was now getting near, at the descent of the Mount of Olives, the whole multitude of the disciples began to rejoice and praise God with a loud voice for all the mighty works which they had seen,
saying, “Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord!  Peace in heaven, and glory in the highest!”
Some of the Pharisees from the multitude said to him, “Teacher, rebuke your disciples!”
He answered them, “I tell you that if these were silent, the stones would cry out.”
b: In this passage we witness the moment Jesus enters Jerusalem. He chooses to ride into the city on a colt, a symbolic act representing peace and humility. The crowd, full of joy and awe at all the miracles Jesus had done, praised God loudly and spread their cloaks on the road to welcome him. The scene shows the glory of Jesus entering his city as Savior.

Jesus' riding in on a donkey shows that he is not a king who rules by force, but a Lord who brings peace and redemption. The scene shows who Jesus is: the promised Messiah and the Son of God, who came into the world not to conquer but to save. Although the Pharisees tried to silence his disciples, Jesus declared that if they were silent, the very stones would cry out, showing his unquestionable sovereignty.

Through this passage God reminds us that Jesus is our Savior, and we should welcome his coming with wholehearted worship. We should not only praise him with our lips but also witness to his love and grace in our lives. Even if the world tries to silence us, we should, like those disciples, boldly bear witness to Jesus.
q: In your life, how do you express worship and praise to Jesus? When the world tries to silence you, how do you boldly bear witness to him?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for giving us Jesus Christ, the King of peace, who brings redemption and hope. Help us boldly witness for him. Whatever the circumstances, may we follow him faithfully and show his glory in our lives. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: When he came near, he saw the city and wept over it,
saying, “If you, even you, had known today the things which belong to your peace! But now, they are hidden from your eyes.
For the days will come on you, when your enemies will throw up a barricade against you, surround you, hem you in on every side,
and will dash you and your children within you to the ground. They will not leave in you one stone on another, because you didn’t know the time of your visitation.”
b: In this passage, as he approaches Jerusalem, Jesus weeps over the city because he foresees the destruction that will come upon it. Jesus sadly sees that the people of Jerusalem did not understand God's care for them or his call to peace, and that a day of judgment and destruction was coming instead. This passage reflects Jesus' deep compassion and grief for those who reject him.

Jesus' weeping shows his love and compassion: he does not want anyone to perish, yet because of their hard hearts and unbelief he foresaw their end. Jerusalem represents those who reject God's salvation and the love of Jesus Christ. Jesus' tears remind us to treasure God's grace and not wait until judgment comes to be sorry.

Through this passage God tells us that he has boundless love and compassion for us, but we must also respond to his call. We need a soft heart that is willing to accept his guidance, so that we avoid falling into unbelief and rebellion and missing the peace and blessing God offers us.
q: In your life, are there times when you have ignored God's call? How can you adjust your attitude and respond to his leading again?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for giving us Jesus Christ, who wept over our souls and who wants us all to have peace. Soften our hearts, so that we do not reject your love, and help us treasure your grace at all times. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: He entered into the temple, and began to drive out those who bought and sold in it,
saying to them, “It is written, ‘My house is a house of prayer,’  but you have made it a ‘den of robbers’!”
He was teaching daily in the temple, but the chief priests, the scribes, and the leading men among the people sought to destroy him.
They couldn’t find what they might do, for all the people hung on to every word that he said.
b: In this passage Jesus enters the temple and sees that it has become a place of buying and selling. Filled with zeal, he drives out those who have made God's house a "den of robbers." Jesus' action shows his regard for the holiness of God's house, and he reminds everyone that the temple should be a house of prayer, not a marketplace.

Jesus' action shows his love for God's work and his refusal to tolerate corruption and injustice. He was not merely cleansing a physical building; he was calling for the cleansing of hearts. He wants people to have reverence before God and to seek fellowship with him sincerely. Although his actions stirred the hostility of the religious leaders, who wanted to destroy him, the people were drawn to Jesus' teaching and recognized the truth he brought.

Through this passage God reminds us that he wants us to keep our hearts pure and to worship him with the right attitude. Does our life, like the temple, need to be continually cleansed by Jesus? Do we keep reverence before God and faithfully obey his word?
q: Does your heart, like the temple, need to be cleansed? How can you keep an attitude of reverence for God in daily life?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for showing us Jesus' zeal and his insistence on holiness. Cleanse our hearts, so that we are always humble in worship and faithful in serving you. May our lives become your dwelling place, full of holiness and reverence. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: On one of those days, as he was teaching the people in the temple and preaching the Good News, the priests and scribes came to him with the elders.
They asked him, “Tell us: by what authority do you do these things? Or who is giving you this authority?”
He answered them, “I also will ask you one question. Tell me:
the baptism of John, was it from heaven, or from men?”
They reasoned with themselves, saying, “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will say, ‘Why didn’t you believe him?’
But if we say, ‘From men,’ all the people will stone us, for they are persuaded that John was a prophet.”
They answered that they didn’t know where it was from.
Jesus said to them, “Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things.”
b: In this passage the religious leaders question Jesus' authority, trying to trap him and find grounds to accuse him. But Jesus answers them wisely by asking whether John's baptism was from heaven or from men. The question put the religious leaders in a dilemma. They were afraid to answer, because whichever they chose, they would expose their own unbelief and hypocrisy.

Jesus' answer shows his wisdom and authority: he was not caught in men's traps, but instead exposed the weakness of those who were trying to attack him. Jesus' authority comes from the Father, and no one can take it away. The silence of the religious leaders reveals the fear and unbelief in their hearts, and reflects their hypocrisy before God.

Through this passage God reminds us that true authority comes from God, and we need to submit to his leading in faith. We should not be like those religious leaders, seeking to entrap or question God's work, but should receive his teaching with humble and reverent hearts. Jesus' wisdom reminds us that when we face challenges, we should hold up God's truth as our shield.
q: When you face challenges in life, do you rely on God's wisdom to make decisions? How can you keep trusting him in hard times?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for giving us Jesus Christ, who showed your wisdom and authority. Give us humble hearts that are willing to submit to your leading and rely on your truth in hard times. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: He began to tell the people this parable. “A  man planted a vineyard, and rented it out to some farmers, and went into another country for a long time.
At the proper season, he sent a servant to the farmers to collect his share of the fruit of the vineyard. But the farmers beat him, and sent him away empty.
He sent yet another servant, and they also beat him, and treated him shamefully, and sent him away empty.
He sent yet a third, and they also wounded him, and threw him out.
The lord of the vineyard said, ‘What shall I do? I will send my beloved son. It may be that seeing him, they will respect him.’
“But when the farmers saw him, they reasoned among themselves, saying, ‘This is the heir. Come, let’s kill him, that the inheritance may be ours.’
They threw him out of the vineyard and killed him. What therefore will the lord of the vineyard do to them?
He will come and destroy these farmers, and will give the vineyard to others.” When they heard that, they said, “May that never be!”
But he looked at them and said, “Then what is this that is written, ‘The stone which the builders rejected was made the chief cornerstone?’
Everyone who falls on that stone will be broken to pieces, but it will crush whomever it falls on to dust.”
b: In this passage Jesus tells a parable about the owner of a vineyard and the unfaithful tenants. The parable represents God (the owner) and the people of Israel (the tenants), along with the prophets (the servants) and Jesus (the beloved son). Through this parable Jesus warns those who reject him that they will finally come under God's judgment. Although God sent prophets again and again to call his people, they refused again and again, and in the end even killed God's Son.

This parable reveals the stubbornness of Israel's leaders and their refusal to accept God's call. Jesus warns them that if they continue in unbelief and rebellion, they will not escape God's judgment. The "stone which the builders rejected" points to Jesus himself, the Christ who was rejected but became the cornerstone. He is the foundation for those who trust in him, but for those who reject him, he becomes the cause of their ruin.

Through this passage God reminds us that his grace is precious, and we must not neglect or reject it. We must be careful not to be like the tenants in the parable and lose God's blessing and grace. Jesus is our cornerstone, and his teaching is the foundation of our faith; we need to build our lives with him at the center.
q: Is your life built on Jesus as its foundation? How can you make sure in daily life that you do not drift from his teaching?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for giving us Jesus Christ, our cornerstone. We ask you to help us faithfully receive his teaching and make him the foundation of our lives. May we be made firm in him and not turn aside from your way. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: The chief priests and the scribes sought to lay hands on him that very hour, but they feared the people—for they knew he had spoken this parable against them.
They watched him and sent out spies, who pretended to be righteous, that they might trap him in something he said, so as to deliver him up to the power and authority of the governor.
They asked him, “Teacher, we know that you say and teach what is right, and aren’t partial to anyone, but truly teach the way of God.
Is it lawful for us to pay taxes to Caesar, or not?”
But he perceived their craftiness, and said to them, “Why do you test me?
Show me a denarius. Whose image and inscription are on it?” They answered, “Caesar’s.”
He said to them, “Then give to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.”
They weren’t able to trap him in his words before the people. They marveled at his answer and were silent.
b: In this passage the religious leaders try to trap Jesus by asking whether it is lawful to pay taxes to Caesar. They expected that whichever way Jesus answered, he would offend one side. But Jesus saw through their scheme and answered wisely: "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's." This answer both defused the enemies' trap and clearly expressed the distinction between the earthly and the spiritual.

Jesus' response shows not only his wisdom but also our responsibilities on earth and in heaven. As citizens of heaven's kingdom, we should respect earthly authorities, but more importantly we must remain loyal to God and give our hearts and lives to him. The religious leaders could find nothing to accuse Jesus of, which shows that he was blameless in word and deed.

Through this passage God reminds us to discern wisely our responsibilities in the world and in spiritual ministry. We need to be responsible citizens on earth, but we must remember that our ultimate loyalty is to God. Everything we have should be given back to him, for he is our Creator and Lord.
q: In your life, how do you balance worldly and spiritual responsibilities? Have you given your life fully to God?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for the wisdom you give to teach us how to live in this world. Help us to be both responsible citizens on earth and faithful servants of yours. May all that we do glorify your name and bear witness to your great power. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: Some of the Sadducees came to him, those who deny that there is a resurrection.
They asked him, “Teacher, Moses wrote to us that if a man’s brother dies having a wife, and he is childless, his brother should take the wife and raise up children for his brother.
There were therefore seven brothers. The first took a wife, and died childless.
The second took her as wife, and he died childless.
The third took her, and likewise the seven all left no children, and died.
Afterward the woman also died.
Therefore in the resurrection whose wife of them will she be? For the seven had her as a wife.”
Jesus said to them, “The children of this age marry, and are given in marriage.
But those who are considered worthy to attain to that age and the resurrection from the dead neither marry nor are given in marriage.
For they can’t die any more, for they are like the angels, and are children of God, being children of the resurrection.
But that the dead are raised, even Moses showed at the bush, when he called the Lord ‘The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.’
Now he is not the God of the dead, but of the living, for all are alive to him.”
Some of the scribes answered, “Teacher, you speak well.”
They didn’t dare to ask him any more questions.
b: In this passage the Sadducees challenge Jesus' teaching on the resurrection, posing a question about marriage in an attempt to stump him. But in his answer Jesus tells them that life after the resurrection is different from life on earth: there is no more marriage there, because resurrection life is eternal, an existence united with God's own life. Jesus went on to cite Moses, pointing out that God is the God of the living, which makes the truth of the resurrection plain.

Jesus' answer reveals the mystery of the kingdom of heaven and the hope of the resurrection. He stresses the holiness and eternity of resurrection life; it is not merely a continuation but a complete change in the very nature of life. Resurrection life goes beyond earthly experience and relationships and enters into an eternal relationship with God. This was a powerful reply to the Sadducees, who did not believe in the resurrection, and showed how they misunderstood the truth of Scripture.

Through this passage God reminds us that the hope of resurrection is one of the central pillars of our faith. We should fix our eyes on eternity and not be confused or misled by the things of this age, but build our lives on God's promises and his eternal truth. The assurance of resurrection gives us strength, so that in the face of death or any challenge we can still look to God with firm hope.
q: In your life, how does the hope of the resurrection affect your decisions and conduct? Have you set the focus of your life on God's eternal promises?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for giving us the hope of resurrection, so that we have confidence and courage on earth. Help us not be entangled by the confusions of this age, but to focus on your promises and eternal life. May our lives reflect your glory, and may we keep trusting you in every challenge. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: He said to them, “Why do they say that the Christ is David’s son?
David himself says in the book of Psalms, ‘The Lord said to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand,
until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet.” ’
“David therefore calls him Lord, so how is he his son?”
b: In this passage Jesus raises a question that challenges the religious leaders' understanding of the Messiah. He quotes the Psalms, pointing out that David called the Christ "Lord," which means that the Christ is far greater than a mere descendant of David. By this Jesus emphasizes that the Messiah is not only a king from David's line but the Son of God, who holds sovereignty in heaven and kingship on earth.

This exchange shows Jesus revealing his own deity and his identity as the Messiah. He is not only the descendant of David that the Jews were expecting, but the Lord who sits at God's right hand with complete sovereignty. Jesus' question challenged the religious leaders' narrow understanding of the Messiah and revealed his true identity and mission.

Through this passage God reminds us that our knowledge of Jesus should not stop at seeing him as a historical figure or a descendant of David, but should recognize him as the Son of God, who holds all authority. We need to establish his lordship in our faith and honor his name in our lives, because he is our Savior and Lord.
q: In your life of faith, how do you establish the lordship of Jesus Christ? How can you honor him better in daily life?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for giving us Jesus Christ, our Lord and Savior. Help us know who he is more deeply and honor him wholeheartedly in our lives. May all that we do reflect our reverence and love for him. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: In the hearing of all the people, he said to his disciples,
“Beware of those scribes who like to walk in long robes, and love greetings in the marketplaces, the best seats in the synagogues, and the best places at feasts;
who devour widows’ houses, and for a pretense make long prayers: these will receive greater condemnation.”
b: In this passage Jesus warns his disciples to beware of the hypocritical scribes. These religious leaders looked devout on the outside and loved to be honored by others, but in private they acted unjustly, even devouring widows' houses. Their conduct was grossly out of keeping with their identity and position, and this hypocrisy will bring a heavier judgment.

Jesus' warning reminds us that true faith is not about outward show or position but about sincerity and righteousness of heart. We cannot merely pursue outward religious ritual or social standing while ignoring what God requires of our hearts. God looks at our motives and our conduct, and he expects us to be genuine and righteous before him.

Through this passage God reminds us that our life of faith should be genuine, the same inside and out. Whatever position we hold, we should act with humility and reverence, staying far from hypocrisy and self-centeredness, because God looks at the heart and will judge all that we do.
q: In your life of faith, are there places where you look devout outwardly but lack sincerity within? How can you be the same inside and out before God?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for teaching us how to live a genuine life of faith. Help us stay far from hypocrisy and pride, and always examine ourselves humbly before you. May our lives be acceptable in your sight. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: He looked up and saw the rich people who were putting their gifts into the treasury.
He saw a certain poor widow casting in two small brass coins.
He said, “Truly I tell you, this poor widow put in more than all of them,
for all these put in gifts for God from their abundance, but she, out of her poverty, put in all that she had to live on.”
b: In this passage Jesus commends a poor widow. She gave only two small coins, yet Jesus said she had put in more than all the rich people, because she gave all that she had to live on. This shows that what God values is the heart behind our giving, not the size of the amount. The widow's offering came from her complete trust in God and her love for him; she held nothing back and gave all she had.

Jesus' words reveal the essence of true giving: it is not about how much we are able to give, but how much we are willing to give, especially when we offer God what is most precious to us. The widow's act showed her faith and her complete dependence on God, which the gifts of the rich could not compare with, because they were only giving out of their surplus.

Through this passage God reminds us that true giving comes not from our abundance but from our hearts. We should reflect on how we use the resources God has given us, and learn from this widow's example, expressing complete trust in and love for God through our giving.
q: In your life of giving, how do you express trust in and love for God? How can you offer yourself to God more sincerely?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for showing us this widow's example, whose giving was full of trust in you and love for you. Teach us how to express our love for you in life, and may our giving, large or small, come from a sincere heart. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.
